# Functions

You wrote the translation loop twice in Chapter 13. The same three lines, once
on `coding` and once on `other_strand`, with four names retyped in between.
Both copies ran. Both did what you told them. So what was wrong with writing it
that way?

<!-- nlr-allow: 1864 -->

## Putting Chapter 13 back on the table

A notebook forgets. Here are four cells from Chapter 13 run as one, with the
two translation loops held back because they're what this chapter is about.
None of it is new, so read it as a receipt rather than as a lesson.

```{python}
table_lines = open("data/codon_table_standard.tsv").read().splitlines()

codon_table = {}
for line in table_lines[1:]:
    codon, amino_acid, name, is_start = line.split("\t")
    codon_table[codon] = amino_acid

text = open("data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta").read()
lines = text.split(">")[1].splitlines()
brca1 = "".join(lines[1:])

coding = brca1[113:5705]

pairing = {"A": "T", "C": "G", "G": "C", "T": "A"}
other_strand = ""
for base in reversed(coding):
    other_strand += pairing[base]

print(len(codon_table), len(coding), len(other_strand))
```

64 codons in the table, and 5,592 bases in each of the two strands of the
coding sequence. Those are Chapter 13's numbers, so the state you had then is
the state you have now.

## What the second copy cost you

Here are the two loops the way you wrote them.

```{python}
translated = ""
for i in range(0, len(coding), 3):
    translated += codon_table[coding[i:i + 3]]

wrong = ""
for i in range(0, len(other_strand), 3):
    wrong += codon_table[other_strand[i:i + 3]]

print(translated[:20])
print(wrong[:20])
```

`translated` became `wrong` in two places, and `coding` became `other_strand`
in two more. You made all four edits by hand, and nothing anywhere checked that
you'd caught them.

Here's the second copy on an evening when you're moving fast.

```{python}
translated = ""
for i in range(0, len(coding), 3):
    translated += codon_table[coding[i:i + 3]]

wrong = ""
for i in range(0, len(coding), 3):
    wrong += codon_table[coding[i:i + 3]]

print(translated[:20])
print(wrong[:20])
```

`other_strand` isn't in that block at all. The two `translated` edits landed
and the two `coding` edits didn't, because `coding` reads correctly wherever
your eye happens to land on it. Nothing errored. What's on screen is a claim
that both strands of *BRCA1* start with the same twenty residues, and the block
above this one shows you they don't.

::: {.trap}
A pasted block runs fine with the old variable name still inside it. Python
can't know which sequence you meant, so you get a clean answer to a question
you didn't ask. Near-identical copies are the dangerous ones: the more alike
two blocks look, the harder it is to spot the line you missed.
:::

The wrong answer isn't the whole cost. Suppose you decide the translator
should stop at the first stop codon rather than read through it. With two
copies you have to remember there are two. With five copies across three
notebooks, you'll fix four and never find the fifth.

## A function is a name for a block you can run again

A [function]{.term def="A block of code with a name. You run the block by
writing the name and a pair of brackets."} is a block of code with a name, so
you can run the block by writing the name instead of the block.

```{python}
def translate(dna):
    translated = ""
    for i in range(0, len(dna), 3):
        translated += codon_table[dna[i:i + 3]]
    return translated


print(translate(coding)[:20])
print(translate(other_strand)[:20])
```

That's Chapter 13's loop with two lines wrapped around it, untouched apart from
the name of the sequence it reads. `def` starts the definition and `translate`
is the name you picked. The indented lines under it are the body, and they
don't run when Python reads them. They run when something calls `translate`.

`dna` in the brackets is a [parameter]{.term def="The name a function gives to
a value it was handed. It exists only while the function is running."}. Write
`translate(coding)` and Python takes whatever `coding` holds and calls it `dna`
for the length of that call. The name inside has nothing to do with the name
outside, so the body can't mention `coding` and there's no stale name left to
forget.

## What comes back

`return translated` hands the string back to whoever called. A call is an
expression that turns into that string, so you can print it or keep it under a
name of your own.

```{python}
translated = translate(coding)

print(len(translated), translated.count("*"), translated[-1])
print(translate(coding[:30]))
```

The `translated` inside the function stopped existing the moment the call
ended. The `translated` on the first line above is a separate name in your
notebook, and it holds what the call handed back.

::: {.check}
The first line reads `1864 1 *`, which is the output Chapter 13's check
asked you for, and it hasn't moved. The second reads `MDLSALRVEE`: ten
characters from 30 bases, no `*` in them. That's the short answer Exercise 13.1
had you predict before you ran anything.
:::

A function with no `return` still runs and still does whatever its body says.
It hands back `None`, which is Python's word for nothing at all. That one
doesn't break where you make it, so it's in the If it breaks section below.

## Walkthrough: the version you can open in six months

Six months from now you'll open this notebook to check a number somebody asked
you about. Three things are obvious to you today and won't be then.

A [docstring]{.term def="A string at the top of a function body, in triple
quotes, saying what the function does and what it assumes."} is a string on the
first line of the body, in triple quotes. Python keeps it, instead of throwing
it away the way it throws away a comment.

```{python}
def translate(dna):
    """Translate a DNA string into one-letter amino acids.

    dna must be upper case, must contain only A, C, G and T, and its
    length must be a multiple of three. Reading starts at the first
    base given, so the reading frame and the strand are the caller's
    problem. Stop codons come back as *.
    """
    translated = ""
    for i in range(0, len(dna), 3):
        translated += codon_table[dna[i:i + 3]]
    return translated


help(translate)
```

`help` prints the docstring of anything that has one, which is how you read a
library you've never used before. The docstring is also the only place those
three assumptions are recorded, because none of them appear anywhere in the
code.

Watch what the function does with the coding sequence read one base later.

```{python}
print(translate(coding[1:43]))
```

That slice is 42 bases, which is 14 codons, so 14 residues come back. No part
of the string says it came from the wrong reading frame, and something like it
could sit in a results table for a year with nobody catching it. The function
did what you asked. The asking was wrong.

::: {.trap}
`translate` will translate any string of A, C, G and T whose length divides by
three. A function takes one line to run, so you'll now point it at sequences
you never checked. The docstring is where the reading-frame assumption gets
written down, because the code won't enforce it and the output won't betray it.
:::

## Exercises

Solutions are in the book's repository under `scripts/solutions/`. Work the
exercise first.

::: {.exercise num="14.1" time="30 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Turn your Chapter 13 translator into one documented function, then prove it
still gives the answers Chapter 13 got.
:::
::: {.given}
Three sequences, all of them already in your notebook: `coding`, its first 30
bases `coding[:30]`, and `other_strand`. Your function takes one parameter and
returns the protein string with its stops left in.
:::
::: {.produce}
The function, carrying a docstring that says what it assumes about its input,
and three printed lines. Each line gives the length of one result, how many
stops it holds, and its first ten characters.
:::
::: {.check}
Every number here is one you already wrote down in Chapter 13. `coding` gives
1,864 characters with one `*`, and it starts `MDLSALRVEE`. Drop that single
stop and you have the 1,863 residues of `NP_009225.1`. The first 30 bases give
`MDLSALRVEE` too, ten characters and no stop. On `other_strand` you get 1,864
characters with 93 stops in them, and 67 residues sit in front of the first
one. If all three still land, the rewrite changed nothing except how many
places you have to edit next time.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()"}
Python is talking here, and the thing it's talking about is the value your
function handed back. `None` means the function ended without a `return`, so
there was nothing to measure. Look at the last line of the body. If it says
`print(translated)`, change it to `return translated` and call the function
again.
:::

::: {.errfix err="TypeError: translate() missing 1 required positional argument: 'dna'"}
You called `translate()` with empty brackets. The definition says the function
needs one value to work on, and Python won't guess which sequence you had in
mind. Put it inside the brackets: `translate(coding)`.
:::

::: {.errfix err="IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1"}
The line after your `def` isn't indented. Indentation is the only thing marking
which lines make up the body, so a definition with nothing indented under it
has no body at all. Put four spaces at the front of every line the function
should run.
:::

::: {.errfix err="NameError: name 'translate' is not defined"}
This one is usually the notebook rather than your code. Either the cell holding
the `def` hasn't been run in this session, or you edited it and ran the call
first. Chapter 4's restart-and-run-all is the reliable answer here. This
chapter downloads nothing, so a full rerun costs you seconds.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Write a function that takes one parameter and returns a value
- Say what a caller gets back from a function whose body has no `return`
- Read a docstring and name what it says the input has to be
- Call one function on three sequences and check each result against a number
  Chapter 13 already gave you
- Point at the line in a pasted block that still names the old variable
:::
